newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. launches cruise missile attacks against Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. launches cruise missile attacks against Iraq.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday launched cruise missile strikes against air defence targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds.
An Iraqi television channel run by President Saddam Hussein's son Uday confirmed the U.S. military strikes announced earlier by the U.S. Defence Department.

"We call the attention of citizens that we are ready to receive calls from them to express their reaction on the latest, vicious American aggression against Iraq," Shabab television said in the first official Iraqi word on an American attack.
Air raid sirens blared in parts of Baghdad, residents said.
"I heard a siren just for a few seconds but could not determine whether it was a warning, a test or sounding all clear," one resident told Reuters.
State-run radio and television interrupted programmes and broadcast national songs.
The Defence Department in Washington said the U.S. raids were launched on orders from President Bill Clinton.

U.S. defence officials said the 25 to 30 unmanned, highly accurate missiles were fired from B-52 bombers and American warships in the Gulf at air defence command and control military targets in and around Baghdad.

The Pentagon statement said: "At the direction of the president, the Department of Defence has launched cruise missiles to attack selected air defence targets in Iraq. No further details are available at this time.

"The president plans to make a formal statement on this operation at approximately 8 a.m. (1200 GMT) this morning. Shortly after the president makes his statement, the secretary of defence and the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff will hold a press conference" at the Pentagon, it added.

In London, British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo told BBC radio: "The Americans have launched a number of military attacks against rural areas. They are purely military targets. They have been selected to minimise collateral damage, that is to say loss of civilian life.

"The no-fly zone in southern Iraq will be extended to allow the allies operating there to have a greater opportunity to control more of Saddam's airspace and bring greater control over him," he added.
In 1993 Clinton launched a cruise missile attack on Iraq in response to its alleged plot to assassinate former president George Bush while Bush was visiting Kuwait that year.
The missiles destroyed an Iraqi intelligence headquarters in central Baghdad where U.S. officials said the plot had been hatched. Six civilians were killed.
An Iraqi opposition group welcomed the U.S. attacks but expressed concern about the possibility of civilian casualties.

"We welcome any action to reverse (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein's invasion of northern Iraq," a spokesman for the Iraqi National Congress (INC) told Reuters. "But we are concerned about civilian casualties. Saddam often puts military facilities in residential areas."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, speaking with reporters earlier as the president campaigned for re-election in Wisconsin, said there was evidence that some of the Iraqi forces that overran the northern Iraqi city of Arbil during the weekend were "penetrating deeper" into northern Iraq.
The advance threatened Sulaimaniya, administrative capital of the Kurdish opposition, he said.
McCurry said there was also reason to believe that some Iraqi troops were involved in executions of leaders of an anti-Baghdad Kurdish faction in Arbil.

The White House believes Saddam sent three tank divisions composed of 30,000-40,000 elite Republican Guard troops into northern Iraq to help the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KPD), involved in a bloody power struggle with another Kurdish group with links to Iran, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
It says U.N. Security Council resolutions approved after the 1991 Gulf War provide the legal basis for responding.
"Our interest is in keeping Saddam Hussein from believing that unjustifiable behaviour of this nature is cost-free," McCurry said.

KDP guerrillas said late on Monday they had made no move to attack Sulaimaniya. "The KDP has no plans to take Sulaimaniya," Sami Abderrahman, a KDP leader, told reporters. Such reports, he said, were a ploy by the PUK.

In Salahuddin in northern Iraq, U.N. officials said Iraqi forces had pulled out of Arbil on Monday after installing a newly allied faction there, and long columns of tanks and other vehicles moved south, U.N. officials said.
But the United States dismissed the redeployment as insignificant.
Saddam's military move and the U.N. decision to delay implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food deal sent the price of crude oil rising on international markets.

Iraqi oil had been expected to start flowing onto world markets in September under a plan that would let Iraq sell $2 billion of oil over six months to buy humanitarian supplies to ease suffering from sanctions imposed after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990.
